newsitem.title: MEXICO: Latam gets growth, but rich-poor divide persists.
newsitem.headline: Latam gets growth, but rich-poor divide persists.

text.p: The good news for Latin America is that economic growth is on its way back, but the bad news is that the rich are still getting richer and the poor are getting poorer.
According to experts at the World Bank and the United Nations, Latin America is set for growth of up to 3 percent in 1996.
But "the sharp inequalities that mark most countries in the region show no sign of diminishing," the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLA) said in a report.
One in every three Latin Americans is poor, with 18 percent or 86 million people suffering extreme poverty, eking out a living on less than $1 per day, a World Bank report released this year said.

The gap between rich and poor varies, with the richest 10 percent in Honduras and Peru having access to about 80 times more resources than the poorest 10 percent. In Uruguay and Barbados the gap is narrowest at around 15 times.
Around Latin America, most leaders see free-market economics, with suitable social spending, as the only way forward.

"It encourages me when we go to the (poor) southeast of Mexico... we start to see businesses dedicated to exporting, generating modern jobs, better paid, and that encourages me that, with this model of open economy, of competition, we can also have a better income distribution," Mexico's President Ernesto Zedillo told Reuters in a recent interview.
The reply from Mexico's hardline rebel left has been straightforward: pass the ammunition.

At least two dozen people died in guerrilla attacks in the second half of 1996 as the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) rebel movement appeared on the scene to demand the overthrow of the government and an end to free-market economics.
In Colombia, too, leftist guerrillas went from strength to strength in 1996.

In Brazil, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said last month that, having slashed inflation in his first two years in office, he now wants to address the gap between rich and poor in his nation of 160 million.

While claiming that defeating inflation alone had lifted 13 million people above the poverty line between 1993 and 1995, Cardoso said agrarian reform was now vital. "It isn't just about raising food production," he said. "It's about whether Brazil starts to pay attention to its dispossesed."
In Chile, a steadily rising tide has not lifted all boats.
After 15 years of solid economic growth, most studies show fewer Chileans living in poverty than when the country returned to democracy in 1990 after 17 years of military rule.

But they also show the income gap between rich and poor widening at a time of record-breaking economic growth -- a trend that worries the government, which now boasts of spending some 50 percent of the budget on social programmes.

A polar opposite to Chile, in many ways the subcontinent's vanguard in terms of economic liberalisation, was Cuba. Sticking doggedly to its communist system, Cuba said growing rich-poor differences across the continent were a result of free-market economics it did not intend to imitate.

The gap between the lowest and highest wages in Cuban pesos remained relatively small -- from a minimum of about 110 pesos a month for a low-paid worker to a maximum of about 500 for a top professional.

But the big difference since hard currency became legal tender in Cuba in 1993 was between Cubans who did not have dollars and those who did, because they had relatives abroad or had jobs involving foreigners.
At the current rate of exchange, a hotel worker making just $100 a month in tips was taking home the equivalent of 2,000 pesos a month, five times the wage of a senior doctor.

Venezuela's middle and upper classes, flush with petro-dollars during the 1970s and 1980s, imported fine caviar and went on weekend shopping trips to Miami, where they were known as "esta barato, deme dos" -- "it's cheap, give me two."

No more. Straight-talking Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff, a left-wing guerrilla in the 1960s but now responsible for leading an ambitious economic reform programme launched in April, said a growing gap between rich and poor in his country was "the mother of all destabilisations."

According to the World Bank report, the number of poor in the region will grow by a million a year, or two people per minute, to a total of 176 million by 2005 if the economic growth and birth rates of the early 1990s persist.

To overcome the income gap and complement economic growth, the World Bank report recommended a "human capital shock" -- stepped-up spending on education to ensure 95 percent of all young people complete basic education and 200 million have access to secondary schooling.

But the bill will not be cheap. The bank estimated the region's nations would need to boost education spending by at least 0.5 percent of gross national product over the next 25 years to have the desired effect.
